summary: Collects and documents machine-readable response codes that IMAP servers can include with OK, NO and BAD replies. Standard codes help clients react correctly and give clearer error reporting across implementations.

plainLanguage.summary: When a mail server says no, a short code can explain why in a way programs understand. This note collects a list of those codes.

subtitle: Seventeen named reasons an IMAP server can give, in a form programs can read, when it says no.

tldr.problem: IMAP servers mostly explained failures in English text, so clients could not tell, for example, a bad password from a broken back-end server.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5530 defines 17 new machine-readable response codes, written in square brackets after OK, NO or BAD, and creates an IANA registry for IMAP response codes.
tldr.outcome: Clients can react correctly and report errors clearly, but no server has to send these codes and no client has to understand them.

facts.label: Required to implement
facts.value: No server or client must test for them

today: RFC 5530 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The IMAP Response Codes registry it created is the place where new codes are recorded.

sections.title: Why More Response Codes
sections.content:
An IMAP reply has a type (OK, NO or BAD), an optional machine-readable response code in square brackets, and human-readable text. RFC 3501 already defines some codes, but experience showed that more are useful. For example, a client benefits from knowing that a login failed because of a server problem rather than a wrong password.

At the time, many servers described errors in English text and a few clients tried to translate it. The codes here come from errors some IMAP server implementations already check for and from the needs of some clients.

The RFC says it does not require servers to test for these errors or clients to test for these names. It only names errors for better reporting and handling.
sections.plainLanguage: Before, the server only wrote a note in words, and a program had to guess what it meant. Now it can also stick on a short label that a program understands.

sections.title: Login and Access Codes
sections.content:
Several codes explain why a user could not get in or act.

  • UNAVAILABLE: a temporary failure because a subsystem is down, such as an LDAP or Radius server used for authentication.
  • AUTHENTICATIONFAILED: authentication failed for a reason the server will not elaborate, typically an unknown user or bad password. Unlike sending no code, it tells the client the cause was not UNAVAILABLE, so retrying the same login and password later is pointless.
  • AUTHORIZATIONFAILED: authentication worked, but the server will not let that identity act as the requested authorization identity. It only applies when the two identities differ.
  • EXPIRED: access is no longer permitted with that passphrase, so the client or user should get a new one.
  • PRIVACYREQUIRED: the operation is not allowed because of a lack of privacy. If TLS is not in use, the client could try STARTTLS and repeat the operation.
  • CONTACTADMIN: the user should contact the system administrator or support desk.
  • NOPERM: the access control system, for example an ACL, does not permit this user to do the operation, such as selecting or creating a mailbox.
sections.plainLanguage: These labels say why the door will not open: the doorman is away, the password is wrong, the password is too old, or you are just not allowed in.

sections.title: Codes About Mailbox Operations
sections.content:
Other codes describe why a command on a mailbox or message did not work as expected.

  • INUSE: someone else holds an exclusive lock, or is using a resource such as a mailbox that the operation would delete. It may succeed if the client tries again later.
  • EXPUNGEISSUED: someone else has issued an EXPUNGE for the same mailbox, so the client may want to issue NOOP soon. It can accompany an OK, as in a completed search.
  • ALREADYEXISTS: the operation tries to create something that already exists, such as a mailbox name taken by CREATE or RENAME.
  • NONEXISTENT: the operation tries to delete or use something that does not exist. It is similar to ALREADYEXISTS.
  • OVERQUOTA: the user would be over quota after the operation. It can come with NO, or with OK when the user is now over a soft quota. If the server lacks the QUOTA extension of RFC 2087, the client cannot find out what the quota is.
  • LIMIT: the operation hit an implementation limit, such as the number of flags on a message or in a mailbox.
sections.plainLanguage: These labels say what went wrong with a mailbox: someone else is using it, the name is taken, it is not there, or it is too full.

sections.title: Codes for Server and Client Faults
sections.content:
A final group blames something specific.

  • CORRUPTION: the server found that relevant data, such as the mailbox, is corrupt. It gives no detail; the server can write that to its logfiles.
  • SERVERBUG: the server hit a bug in itself or violated one of its own invariants.
  • CLIENTBUG: the server detected a client bug. It can accompany OK, NO and BAD, depending on the bug.
  • CANNOT: the operation violates some invariant of the server and can never succeed, for example creating a mailbox named with adjacent slashes.

The difference between CANNOT and, say, INUSE matters to a client: the first will never work, while the second may work later.
sections.plainLanguage: These labels say whose fault it was: the server's, the client's, or that the request can never work no matter what.

sections.title: Formal Syntax and Examples
sections.content:
The RFC extends the resp-text-code rule from RFC 3501 using ABNF from RFC 5234, adding all 17 names. Except as noted, alphabetic characters are case-insensitive.

Each code is shown with example lines marked C: for the client and S: for the server, such as a failed login answered with NO [UNAVAILABLE].
sections.plainLanguage: The note also writes down exactly how the labels are spelled so every program reads them the same way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC warns against revealing information about a passphrase to unauthenticated clients. It also notes that response codes are easier to parse than text, which can amplify an information leak.

Its example: selecting a mailbox can fail because it does not exist, or because the user lacks the "l" right (to know it exists) or the "r" right (to read it). If a server once sent different responses for those cases, only malicious clients would notice. With codes, benevolent clients will probably forward leaked information to the user. Server authors are encouraged to be particularly careful with NOPERM and authentication-related responses.
sections.plainLanguage: Labels are easy for programs to read, so a label that gives away too much, like 'that user exists', gets noticed more. Servers should be careful what they reveal.

sections.title: The IMAP Response Codes Registry
sections.content:
IANA created an IMAP Response Codes registry and populated it with the codes from this RFC plus many from earlier RFCs, such as ALERT, UIDVALIDITY and TRYCREATE from RFC 3501. NEWNAME from RFC 2060 is listed as obsolete.

New codes are requested from IANA, which forwards the request to a Designated Expert. After 30 days of community input on the IMAP Extensions mailing list or a successful IETF Last Call, the expert approves or rejects it. The intent is that each allocation comes with a published RFC, though the expert may approve early once publication seems clear. The expert can also register codes used in deployed software when no RFC exists, marked "reserved to prevent collision with deployed software".

Registrations may not be deleted; codes no longer believed appropriate should be marked "obsolete". A status description means the code is NOT RECOMMENDED for widespread use.
sections.plainLanguage: There is now an official list of all the labels. To add a new one you ask a referee, who checks that it makes sense.

messages.note: The client tries to log in.
